summary: Describes a general architecture for running IPv6 over non-broadcast multiple access networks, where machines cannot simply shout to everyone. It is a proposed standard and was updated by RFC 8064.

eli5.summary: Some networks cannot send one message to everyone at once. This explains how IPv6 still works on them.

questions: how does ipv6 work over nbma networks
what is the ipv6 nbma architecture
what is a logical link in ipv6 over nbma
what is a transient neighbor in ipv6
subtitle: An architecture for running IPv6 Neighbor Discovery on networks that cannot broadcast, with optional direct shortcuts.

tldr.problem: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery assumes the link can multicast, but NBMA networks such as ATM or Frame Relay cannot do that natively, and routing every packet hop by hop wastes the network's ability to connect endpoints directly.
tldr.mechanism: A set of nodes is configured as a Logical Link, and MARS emulates multicast inside it so Neighbor Discovery works unchanged. Routers use NHRP and Redirect messages to set up direct shortcut connections across Logical Links.
tldr.outcome: It is a general framework that leaves technology-specific details to companion documents. It is a Proposed Standard, later updated by RFC 8064.

today: RFC 2491 is a Proposed Standard that has been updated by RFC 8064; it has not been obsoleted. Technology-specific details live in companion documents such as RFC 2492 for ATM.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
A Non-Broadcast Multiple Access (NBMA) network can be used simply, as administratively configured point-to-point links. At the other extreme it can set up and tear down Virtual Circuits dynamically and emulate a broadcast medium such as Ethernet. That emulation usually needs complex convergence protocols, especially for IPv6 multicast.

This RFC describes a general architecture for IPv6 over NBMA. It is the base for companion documents covering specific technologies, for example RFC 2492 for ATM. Dynamic calls are called SVCs and administratively configured ones PVCs. Most of the document is about the SVC case.

The key difference from earlier approaches is how Neighbor Discovery is handled. IPv4 used a link-specific helper such as ARP (RFC 826). IPv6 chose a link-independent Neighbor Discovery protocol that assumes native multicast. Here, the MARS protocol (RFC 2022) is augmented to supply that multicast, so hosts run ordinary Neighbor Discovery.

For PVC-only use, each PVC connects exactly two nodes, so a node has one neighbor per link. MARS and NHRP are not needed and shortcuts are not supported.
sections.eli5: On a network where you can only phone one person at a time, a special helper repeats a message to everyone who needs it. Then the computers can talk the usual IPv6 way.

sections.title: Logical Links and Transient Neighbors
sections.content:
IPv6 divides the world into on-link and off-link. On NBMA, the equivalent of the IPv4 Logical IP Subnet is the Logical Link (LL): a set of nodes administratively configured to be on-link with each other. LL members are an interface's initial neighbors, and its link-local address only needs to be unique among them.

Neighbor Discovery events can add neighbors outside the LL without changing LL membership. That gives three relationships between two interfaces: on LL and a neighbor, off LL and a neighbor, or off LL and not a neighbor. An off-LL neighbor represents a shortcut: a direct NBMA-level call between two endpoints separated by one or more IP routers. Neighbors learned from unsolicited messages such as Redirects are called Transient Neighbors.

Shortcuts save resources such as router hops and NBMA virtual circuits. The RFC says they should be supported whenever IP runs over NBMA networks that can set up calls dynamically.
sections.eli5: A Logical Link is a friend group. Sometimes you also get a direct line to someone outside the group, and that person is a temporary neighbor.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery Inside a Logical Link
sections.content:
An IPv6 LL maps directly onto an IPv6 MARS Cluster, just as an IPv4 LIS maps onto an IPv4 MARS Cluster. The IPv6 layer simply passes multicast ICMPv6 packets down to the driver, with no NBMA-specific handling, and the MARS spreads them.

A node must first set up a point-to-point VC to its MARS and register as a Cluster Member. A host or router then issues a group MARS_JOIN for its solicited-node address(es), the All-nodes address and any other configured groups of at least link-local scope. Routers also join the All-routers address and may block-join ranges of larger-scope multicast addresses. Joins and leaves for node-local addresses need no action, because those packets never reach the driver.

Certain multicast packets are sent straight to the MARS over the node's point-to-point VC: link-local solicited-node, All-nodes and All-routers destinations, and DHCPv6 relay or server addresses. When the MARS receives such a packet it looks up the group members. If every member has an open point-to-point VC to the MARS, it sends each a copy there. Otherwise, or if no members are listed, it sends the packet on ClusterControlVC instead. All other multicast packets use the normal MARS client mechanisms.
sections.eli5: When someone wants to shout to the group, they give the message to a helper, the MARS. The helper hands copies to each member, or announces it on a line everybody listens to.

sections.title: Shortcuts with Redirects and NHRP
sections.content:
A shortcut starts with a Redirect message, which tells a host there is a better first hop and can carry that hop's NBMA address. A host acts only on Redirects from its current default router for that destination. It updates its Neighbor Cache entry, sets it to STALE, and builds a new VC to the new address. The old VC is torn down only if it is no longer needed.

Two triggers exist. In flow-triggered redirection (optional for routers), the router tracks flows from directly attached hosts, never uses packets arriving from another router, and considers only packets whose FlowID is zero. It keeps forwarding normally while it asks NHRP for a better hop. Detection must be switchable off by an administrator. A non-zero FlowID suppresses it so hosts can opt out of the network's own optimizing.

In host-triggered redirection, the host sends a Neighbor Solicitation for the off-LL target to its next-hop router, with hop limit 255 and a shortcut limit option equal to the hop limit of the data flow. If the router does not do shortcut discovery, it answers with a Redirect naming itself. If it does, it sends an NHRP Request, turns the Reply into a Redirect carrying the NBMA address, and the host then treats the target as a Transient Neighbor.

Routers use NHRP in NHS-to-NHS mode. The Request follows the routed path toward the target, so the shortcut is bounded by the scope of the target address. The last-hop router answers from its Neighbor cache, or performs Neighbor Discovery if needed. It returns the NBMA address the target chose when the flow was first accepted, which keeps the destination's ability to share load across its interfaces. NHRP replies carry a holding time of 10 minutes. If NHRP later sends a Purge, the router must issue a Redirect naming itself as the new best next hop.
sections.eli5: A router that notices lots of traffic between two far-apart computers can find out their direct phone number and tell the sender to call that number instead of going through every middleman.

sections.title: Sending Data and Managing VCs
sections.content:
For NBMA networks that normally use LLC/SNAP (such as ATM or SMDS), unicast IPv6 packets are sent over a point-to-point VC with an LLC/SNAP header carrying the EtherType 0x86DD. Multicast packets use a longer header that includes the sender's 2-octet Cluster Member ID. A receiver silently drops a multicast packet whose Cluster Member ID matches its own, which prevents it from seeing its own transmission echoed back. Networks that do not use LLC/SNAP must define alternative rules in their companion document.

If no VC exists to the next hop, the node places a call, and SHOULD queue the triggering packet. If the call fails the packet is discarded, and persistent failure is left to Neighbor Unreachability Detection. Unicast VCs are best effort only.

An IPv6/NBMA driver SHALL release any VC idle for 20 minutes, which may be reduced by configuration or companion documents. Purged or STALE Neighbor and Destination cache entries SHOULD cause their VCs to be released. Redirects are unidirectional, so the redirected node uses the new VC but the destination keeps replying on the old path. Drivers must negotiate acceptable MTUs per VC using mechanisms defined in companion documents.
sections.eli5: Each call is hung up after 20 quiet minutes. If you were redirected to a new line, only you use it; the other side keeps using the old one until it hears about it too.

sections.title: Interface Tokens and Address Options
sections.content:
Each interface needs an interface token to build autoconfigured addresses. It must be unique within a Logical Link, be exactly 64 bits, and be based on the EUI-64 format. If two nodes on one LL collide, one must choose another token, and implementations MUST support manual configuration of tokens. How tokens are generated for a given NBMA technology is left to companion documents. A host with separate interfaces on different LLs can reuse one token because the routing prefixes differ, but virtual hosts sharing a driver on one LL must each get a unique token.

The link-layer address option is adapted from MARS and NHRP: a Type (1 for source, 2 for target), a Length in multiples of 8 octets, NTL and STL one-octet fields, a variable-length NBMA number and an optional NBMA subaddress, zero-padded to a multiple of 8 octets. The meaning of NTL, STL and the address fields is technology specific. The link-local address is the token appended to FE80::/64.
sections.eli5: Every computer needs a name tag unique within its group. The address label has room for a main number and an optional extension, like a phone number plus extension.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The architecture introduces no new protocols, so it inherits the threats of the protocols it uses: NHRP, IPv6, Neighbor Discovery and MARS. It should not be used in a domain where any of them is considered unacceptably insecure. The RFC says existing IPv6 security mechanisms, including authentication and encryption for Neighbor Discovery and for data packets, work without modification over NBMA. The MARS change does not affect the security offered by RFC 2022.
sections.eli5: This adds no new locks and no new weak spots. It is only as safe as the pieces it is built from.

messages.label: IPv6 flow
messages.note: FlowID is zero; the router keeps forwarding it normally.

messages.label: NHRP Request
messages.note: Asks for the NBMA address of the flow's destination.

messages.label: NHRP Reply
messages.note: Carries the target's preferred NBMA address.

messages.label: Redirect
messages.note: Names the destination as a Transient Neighbor.

fields.name: Shortcut Limit
fields.desc: Hop limit for the shortcut attempt, relative to the requesting host.

fields.name: Reserved1
fields.desc: Sender sets to zero; receiver ignores it.

fields.desc: Sender sets to zero; receiver ignores it.
